Optimal dispatch of energy storage systems (ESSs) in distri bution networks involves jointly improv-
ing operating economy and voltage security under time-vary ing conditions and possible topology
changes. To support fast online decision making, we develop a topology-aware Reinforcement
Learning architecture based on Twin Delayed Deep Determini stic Policy Gradient (TD3), which
integrates graph neural networks (GNNs) as graph feature en coders for ESS dispatch. We conduct
a systematic investigation of three GNN variants: graph con volutional networks (GCNs), topology
adaptive graph convolutional networks (TAGConv), and grap h attention networks (GATs) on the
34-bus and 69-bus systems, and evaluate robustness under mu ltiple topology reconﬁguration cases
as well as cross-system transfer between networks with diﬀe rent system sizes. Results show that
GNN-based controllers consistently reduce the number and m agnitude of voltage violations, with
clearer beneﬁts on the 69-bus system and under reconﬁgurati on; on the 69-bus system, TD3-GCN
and TD3-TAGConv also achieve lower saved cost relative to th e NLP benchmark than the NN
baseline. We also highlight that transfer gains are case-de pendent, and zero-shot transfer between
fundamentally diﬀerent systems results in notable perform ance degradation and increased volt-
age magnitude violations. This work is available at: https://github.com/ShuyiGao/GNNs_RL_ESSs and
https://github.com/distributionnetworksTUDelft/GNNs _RL_ESSs .
1. Introduction
The increasing penetration of distributed energy re-
sources (DERs), together with time-varying electricity pr ices,
has made real-time operation of distribution networks (DNs )
increasingly challenging [ 1]. High penetration of DERs
introduces uncertainty, variability, and bidirectional p ower
ﬂows, while price volatility requires timely decisions be-
cause economically preferred actions can change over short
intervals [ 2]. In particular, distribution network operation
must jointly maintain energy balance, reduce operating cos t,
and satisfy voltage and device constraints, which makes
practical operation a tightly coupled constrained dispatc h
problem that co-optimizes economic objectives with net-
work security [ 3]. Energy storage systems (ESSs) provide a
key source of ﬂexibility in distribution networks by enabli ng
temporal energy shifting, smoothing net-load ﬂuctuations ,
and supporting local voltage regulation [ 4]. Accordingly,
ESS dispatch is commonly formulated as an optimization
problem that coordinates charging/discharging decisions
with network and device constraints, such as voltage limits ,
line constraints, and state-of-charge (SOC) dynamics, whi ch
often leads to non-linear programming (NLP) formulations.
Model-based optimizations, such as stochastic programmin g
[5,6,7] and robust optimization [ 8,9] can deliver high-
quality solutions; however, repeatedly solving them in rea l
time can be computationally demanding, particularly for
large networks or when operating conditions change fre-
quently [ 10].

sensors further enhances the viability of data-driven Rein -
forcement Learning (RL) as an alternative for operational
decision making [ 11]. The optimization problem of ESS
dispatch can be formulated as a Markov decision process
(MDP), and solved using powerful data-driven RL algo-
rithms. In detail, by training oﬄine with a simulator and
executing online with a forward pass of the policy network,
RL can provide near-instant control actions, alleviating t he
latency bottleneck of repeatedly solving complex optimiza -
tions [ 12]. Accordingly, RL has been increasingly explored
for distribution network operation, including ESS dispatc h
[13,14,15] and voltage regulation [ 16,17], and open-source
toolkits [ 18,19] have been developed to facilitate research
and benchmarking.
Despite these advances, two challenges remain in dis-
tribution networks. First, voltage regulation is topology -
dependent: the impact of ESS actions on voltages is gov-
erned by electrical connectivity and line impedances, and
becomes harder to capture in deeper, more heterogeneous
networks [ 20]. Second, distribution networks frequently ex-
perience topology reconﬁguration due to switching opera-
tions and service restoration, which alters coupling among
buses [ 21]. As a result, topology-agnostic controllers may
generalize poorly and yield inconsistent constraint satis fac-
tion, motivating graph-structured learning models.
Distribution networks naturally form graphs of buses
and lines, making graph neural networks (GNNs) a natural
choice for representation learning [ 22]. By performing mes-
sage passing over the grid topology, GNNs learn graph em-
beddings from node features, which motivates the following
advantages over topology-agnostic neural networks(NNs):

•Spatial awareness of physical relationships
GNNs inherently capture spatial dependencies and lo-
cal interactions between physically connected nodes,
which aligns with the network nature and physical
constraints (e.g., power ﬂow) of energy systems [ 23].
•Eﬃcient learning on large networks
Compared with topology-agnostic NNs that rely on
ﬂattened states, GNNs leverage sparse connectivity
and shared local aggregation, which becomes increas-
ingly advantageous in larger and more heterogeneous
networks by preserving topology information without
a dense representation [ 24].
•Transferability across heterogeneous networks
GNNs have the potential to generalize to unseen or
reconﬁgured topologies under consistent node feature
deﬁnitions [ 25], whereas NN-based controllers built
on ﬁxed-size representations are typically tied to a
speciﬁc input dimension and can be less ﬂexible when
the network size changes.
This makes GNNs especially suitable for RL-based
ESSs dispatch, and has motivated the recent development of
topology-aware RL frameworks. For example, [ 2] proposed
a graph-based RL framework for real-time optimal schedul-
ing in active distribution networks, using a graph attentio n
network (GAT) module to encode topology-aware states
and classic actor-critic based RL deep deterministic polic y
gradient (DDPG) to generate control actions. Experiments
on a modiﬁed IEEE 33-bus system under fault scenarios
showed improved scheduling performance and adaptability
to topology variations. Similarly, [ 26] proposes an RL
approach with a GAT-based topology encoder for voltage
regulation in distribution networks. Tests on IEEE 33-nodeand 136-node systems demonstrated faster convergence
and better voltage control performance than existing RL
baselines, while a GNN-RL based dynamic reconﬁguration
optimization model for energy storage management under
faults and varying network scenarios has been proposed
in [27]. Case studies reported improved decision accuracy,
reduced voltage violations, and enhanced operational se-
curity. In [ 28], a two-stage voltage regulation framework
is presented, combining day-ahead mixed-integer second-
order cone optimization programming (MISOCP) and a
real-time graph convolutional network (GCN) based RL
controller for fast voltage magnitude support. Simulation s
showed eﬀective mitigation of voltage magnitude ﬂuctua-
tions with real-time applicability. Nevertheless, the abo ve-
mentioned works typically adopt a single GNN architecture
and rarely provide systematic comparisons of diﬀerent GNN
variants against standard NN baselines or systematic trans fer
tests across multiple topology reconﬁguration cases. For
practical deployment, an RL controller should jointly deli ver
strong economic performance, minimize voltage magnitude
violations, and be robust to topology changes. This motivat es
a comprehensive evaluation of GNN-based RL for ESS op-
timal dispatch, through consistent comparisons across GNN
architectures, network sizes, and reconﬁguration scenari os.
To this end, this paper introduces a topology-aware
GNN-based RL architecture for optimal dispatch of ESSs in
distribution networks, thoroughly evaluated under both ec o-
nomic and voltage-related metrics. The main contributions
are summarized as follows:
• We develop a topology-aware graph feature encoder
for ESS dispatch, and integrate three representa-
tive GNNs: graph convolutional networks (GCN),

embeddings that incorporate network topology and
electrical coupling.
• We integrate the graph feature encoder into TD3 with
asymmetric actor-critic representations: the actor uses

• We systematically assess robustness and general-

topology reconﬁguration cases within each system
and cross-system transfer between networks of diﬀer-

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section 2models the ESS optimal dispatch problem as an
NLP formulation and formulates it in to an MDP. Section 3
introduces the proposed GNN-based RL framework, includ-
ing the proposed graph feature encoder and the actor-critic
training procedure. Section 4presents experimental settings
and evaluation metrics, discusses the results on the 34-
bus and 69-bus systems, including convergence, operationa l
behavior, voltage magnitude regulation, and topology reco n-
ﬁguration transfer. Finally, Section 5concludes the paper
and outlines future work.

4. Case Study
The experiments are conducted in an open-source envi-
ronment [ 19] that simulates the dispatch of ESSs in distri-
bution networks. A day-ahead operation horizon with a 15-
min resolution is considered, resulting in 96 decision step s
for a single operating day. To investigate the eﬀectiveness
of GNNs in ESS energy dispatch and voltage magnitude
regulation, two benchmark distribution systems, i.e., the 34-
bus system and the 69-bus system, are adopted. These two
networks diﬀer in topology complexity and scale, enabling
a systematic evaluation of the learning performance and
generalization capability of the proposed GNN-based polic y
under diﬀerent grid conditions. The ESSs are set on nodes
{12,16,27,30,34}in the 34-bus system, and are modeled
with an energy capacity of 500kWh and a maxium charg-
ing/discharging power of 200kW. For the 69-bus system,
ESSs are set on nodes {14,16,18,20,22,24,26,27,65}, the
energy capacity is 1000 kWh and a power rating of 300kW.In both cases, the charging/discharging eﬃciencies are set
to/u1D702/u1D456= 1, and the SOC is constrained within [0.2,0.8]with
initial SOC as 0.4.
All training experiments were performed on the Delft
Blue high-performance computing (HPC) system [ 37]. To
reduce stochastic bias and improve reproducibility, each
setting is repeated with ﬁve random seeds, and the reported
results are averaged across seeds. All the RL algorithms
share the same setting of hyperparameters with a learning
rate of6/u1D452− 5, discount factor /u1D6FE= 0.995, a replay buﬀer
size of 1e6, a batch size of 512, and soft target updates with
/u1D70F= 5/u1D452− 3. Target policy smoothing is enabled with noise

For the TD3-NN, the actor and critic adopt the same
multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) size with 3 fully-connected
layers and 256 hidden units per layer (ReLU activations), an d
the critic follows the standard twin-Q design. For the GNN-
based TD3, the actor and critic are implemented as two
separate graph networks with the same depth. Both networks
consist of 3 graph layers, where the hidden dimensions
are set to 64. For the actor, the ESS nodes’ embeddings
are mapped to actions by an MLP with 2 hidden layers of
256-units, followed by a tanh(⋅)output to bound actions

For performance benchmarking, RL policies are com-
pared against a global optimization baseline implemented i n
Pyomo, where the ESS dispatch problem is formulated as

perfect knowledge of the future input proﬁles (e.g., day-

an optimistic reference under the assumed model accuracy.

34-bus and 69-bus systems, including tests under topology

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This document introduces a novel approach to optimal dispatch of Energy Storage Systems (ESSs) in distribution networks using Topology-Aware Graph Reinforcement Learning (RL). The main points covered are:

*   **Problem Formulation:** The optimal dispatch of ESSs is framed as a complex optimization problem that aims to improve operating economy and voltage security under dynamic conditions and potential topology changes in distribution networks.
*   **Proposed Solution:** A topology-aware RL architecture is developed, integrating Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) as feature encoders within an asymmetric actor-critic RL framework (specifically, Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient - TD3). This architecture is designed to capture both local actions and system-wide voltage effects.
*   **GNN Variants Explored:** The study systematically investigates three GNN variants: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), Topology Adaptive Graph Convolutional Networks (TAGConv), and Graph Attention Networks (GATs).
*   **Key Benefits of Topology-Aware RL:**
    *   **Reduced Voltage Violations:** The topology-aware RL approach significantly reduces the frequency and magnitude of voltage violations.
    *   **Improved Performance on Larger Systems and Reconfigurations:** Clearer benefits are observed on larger systems (like the 69-bus system) and under network reconﬁguration scenarios.
    *   **Economic Gains:** In some cases (e.g., 69-bus system), the GNN-based controllers achieve lower saved costs compared to traditional Non-Linear Programming (NLP) benchmarks and standard Neural Network (NN) RL baselines.
*   **Transferability and Generalization:** The research highlights that transfer benefits are case-dependent. Cross-system zero-shot transfer (applying a model trained on one network to a different, fundamentally different network) leads to performance degradation and increased voltage violations.

structure.title: Experiments and Results:
structure.summary:
The document discusses the implementation of graph neural networks (GNNs) within a reinforcement learning (RL) framework, specifically using the TD3 algorithm, for energy storage system (ESS) dispatch in distribution networks.

The main points covered are:

*   **Graph Representation:** The learned graph representation captures both structural information and node features, allowing for transferability across different network topologies.
*   **Graph Message Passing Layers:** Three GNN architectures are explored for implementing the message-passing function:
    *   **GCNConv:** Aggregates neighbor information using a normalized adjacency matrix, suitable for fixed topologies like power systems.
    *   **TAGConv:** Extends GCNConv by incorporating K-order polynomial filters for multi-hop aggregation, capturing both local and global structures.
    *   **GATConv:** Uses an attention mechanism to assign different weights to neighbors, allowing the model to focus on relevant connections and adaptively emphasize influential nodes.
*   **Reinforcement Learning Algorithm (TD3):** The TD3 algorithm is employed for handling continuous actions with improved stability and sample efficiency, utilizing a replay buffer. The document details the TD3 training workflow, including action generation, target policy smoothing, and network updates.
*   **Case Study:** Experiments are conducted on two benchmark distribution systems (34-bus and 69-bus) to evaluate the effectiveness of GNNs in ESS energy dispatch and voltage magnitude regulation.
*   **Performance Comparison:**
    *   **Training Performance:** GNN-based RL agents generally show improved performance on the more complex 69-bus system compared to a non-graph-based TD3 (TD3-NN), while TD3-NN performs well on the simpler 34-bus system. TD3-GATConv exhibits sensitivity to random seeds.
    *   **Dispatch Actions and SOC Trajectories:** The learned policies are compared against an NLP baseline, with GNN-based methods showing comparable or improved dispatch actions and State of Charge (SOC) trajectories.
    *   **Voltage Magnitude Regulation:** GNN-based methods consistently achieve fewer voltage violations than TD3-NN, indicating that topology-aware representations improve constraint satisfaction.
    *   **Training and Execution Time:** GNN-based agents have longer training times due to message passing but offer significantly faster execution times compared to traditional optimization methods.
    *   **Economic Performance:** GNN-based methods achieve comparable or better cost savings than TD3-NN, especially on the 69-bus system.
*   **Trade-offs among GNN Variants:** Different GNN architectures exhibit trade-offs between economic performance and voltage constraint satisfaction, with TAGConv and GATConv showing a better balance.
